Call Break Rules, Scoring and Strategy

Call Break is a four-player trick-taking game with spades as permanent trumps. Here is everything you need to play — and to score it correctly.

Keeping score? Open the Call Break score tracker — it does the maths for you.

Players and cards

Four players each play for themselves with a standard 52-card deck. Cards rank A (high), K, Q, J, 10 down to 2. Spades are always trumps. A game is usually 5 rounds (deals), and the deal passes to the right after each round.

Dealing

The dealer shuffles and deals all 52 cards, one at a time, so everyone holds 13. Many groups allow a redeal if a player has no spades, or no card higher than a 10 — agree on this before you start.

Calling (bidding)

Starting with the player to the dealer's right, each player calls the number of tricks they expect to win, from 1 to 13. Each player calls once; there is no raising. The calls do not need to add up to 13 — they usually don't.

Playing the tricks

  • The player to the dealer's right leads the first trick. The winner of each trick leads the next.
  • You must follow suit if you can.
  • In most Nepali games you must also try to win the trick: if you can beat the highest card played so far, you must.
  • If you can't follow suit, you must play a spade (trump) if you have one — and beat an earlier spade if you can.
  • If you have neither the led suit nor a spade, play any card.
  • The highest spade wins the trick; if no spade was played, the highest card of the suit led wins.

How scoring works

After all 13 tricks:

  • Made your call (won at least as many tricks as you called): score your call, plus 0.1 for each extra trick.
  • Missed your call: lose points equal to your call.

Scores are added up over the rounds. After the last round, the player with the highest total wins.

Common house rules

  • Big call bonus: some groups give 13 points to a player who calls 8 or more and makes it.
  • Maximum call: some groups cap calls at 8.
  • Number of rounds: 5 is standard, but you can set any number in the tracker.

Bidding strategy

  • Count sure winners first. The ace of spades is a certain trick. Side-suit aces usually win, especially in suits where you hold only two or three cards.
  • Long spades are worth tricks. With five or more spades, your lower spades often win once others run out.
  • Shortness is power. A void or a single card in a side suit lets you trump early — count roughly one trick per spare spade you can use this way.
  • Kings and queens are shaky. A king without its ace is a coin flip; a lone queen rarely wins. Value them cautiously.
  • Missing costs more than overshooting. Missing a call of 5 costs 10 points of swing compared with making it; an extra trick only gives 0.1. When in doubt, call one less.
  • Use your position. The last player to call knows the total so far. If the calls already add up to 13 or more, tricks will be fought for — call conservatively.
  • Mind the scoreboard. In the last round, a player who is behind may need to call aggressively; a leader can call safely.

Frequently asked questions

How is Call Break scored?

If you win at least as many tricks as you called, you score your call plus 0.1 for each extra trick. If you win fewer, you lose points equal to your call. For example, call 4 and win 5 scores 4.1; call 4 and win 3 scores −4.

How many rounds are in a game of Call Break?

The standard game is 5 rounds. The player with the highest total after the last round wins. Some groups play more rounds by agreement.

What is the minimum and maximum call in Call Break?

The minimum call is 1. The maximum is 13, although some groups cap calls at 8.

Do you have to win the trick if you can in Call Break?

In most Nepali rules, yes: you must follow suit and play a higher card if you have one, and if you can't follow suit you must trump with a spade.

What happens if a player has no spades?

Many groups allow a redeal if any player's hand has no spades or no face cards. Agree on this rule before the game starts.
